``` # Learning objectives and overview This course introduces the principles of statistical testing through examples of commonly used tests. The examples draw on data from Gapminder and are illustrated with R and Python code. By the end of this session, you should be able to: - understand how statistical tests work; - test the distribution of a variable; - choose an appropriate test; - carry out tests in R or Python; - interpret the results of a test. # Data ## Gapminder data Gapminder provides a wide range of demographic, economic, social and environmental indicators for countries around the world. ### Exploring Gapminder data Explore how the relationship between gross domestic product (GDP) and life expectancy (`lex`) has changed since 1800. We will then work with these variables. ```{=html}

This video is available in the HTML version of the course.* ::: ### Drawing a random sample of `pop` values Here we randomly select 50 countries for which population data are available. ::: {#cell-random-pop-sample .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 5 # Exclude only missing population values, then sample 50 countries without replacement. data_filtre = data_2025.dropna(subset=["pop"]) echantillon_pop = data_filtre.sample(n=50, replace=False, random_state=123) resultat = echantillon_pop[["name", "region", "pop"]] display(resultat.head(10)) ``` ::: {#random-pop-sample .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### A histogram of the sample ::: {#cell-histogram-random-pop .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 6 plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4)) plt.hist(echantillon_pop["pop"], bins=15, color="steelblue", edgecolor="white", density=False) plt.title('Random sample of 50 countries') plt.xlabel('Population (people)') plt.ylabel('Number of countries') plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Population distribution in a random sample of 50 countries.](index-en_files/figure-html/histogram-random-pop-output-1.png){#histogram-random-pop width=663 height=374} ::: ::: ## How statistical tests work A statistical test usually starts with two hypotheses: - **H0**, the null hypothesis: no effect, no difference or no departure from a reference distribution; - **H1**, the alternative hypothesis: an effect, a difference or a departure from that distribution. The **p-value** is the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming that H0 is true. At the commonly used significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$: - if `p < 0.05`, we reject H0; - if `p >= 0.05`, we do not have sufficient evidence to reject H0. ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} ```{=html}

``` [Open the video](https://mediaserver.unige.ch/play/319449). ::: ::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"} *From population to decision. This video is available in the HTML version of the course.* ::: We randomly generate 50 observations from a standard normal distribution, visualise their distribution and apply the **Shapiro–Wilk test**. For this test: - H0: the data are consistent with a normal distribution; - H1: the data are not consistent with a normal distribution. ::: {#cell-normal-sample .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 7 rng = np.random.default_rng(123) echantillon_normal = rng.normal(loc=0, scale=1, size=50) plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4)) plt.hist(echantillon_normal, bins=12, color="steelblue", edgecolor="white", density=False) plt.title('Sample of 50 values: normal') plt.xlabel('Value') plt.ylabel('Count') plt.tight_layout() plt.show() test_normalite = stats.shapiro(echantillon_normal) print(f"W = {test_normalite.statistic:.4f}, p-value = {test_normalite.pvalue:.3g}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index-en_files/figure-html/normal-sample-output-1.png){#normal-sample width=663 height=374} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` W = 0.9803, p-value = 0.565 ``` ::: ::: ### Example 2: a sample from a uniform distribution ::: {#cell-uniform-sample .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 8 rng = np.random.default_rng(123) echantillon_uniforme = rng.uniform(low=0, high=1, size=50) plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4)) plt.hist(echantillon_uniforme, bins=12, color="steelblue", edgecolor="white", density=False) plt.title('Sample of 50 values: uniform') plt.xlabel('Value') plt.ylabel('Count') plt.tight_layout() plt.show() test_normalite = stats.shapiro(echantillon_uniforme) print(f"W = {test_normalite.statistic:.4f}, p-value = {test_normalite.pvalue:.3g}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index-en_files/figure-html/uniform-sample-output-1.png){#uniform-sample width=663 height=374} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` W = 0.9162, p-value = 0.00172 ``` ::: ::: **Keep in mind:** with only 50 observations, a normality test may fail to detect a departure from normality. Interpret the test alongside the graphs. ### Example 3: testing the normality of `gdp` ::: {#cell-shapiro-gdp .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 9 gdp_complete = data_2025['gdp_pcap'].dropna() print("n =", len(gdp_complete)) plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4)) plt.hist(gdp_complete, bins=30, color="steelblue", edgecolor="white", density=False) plt.title('Distribution of GDP per capita') plt.xlabel('GDP per capita') plt.ylabel('Number of countries') plt.tight_layout() plt.show() test_normalite = stats.shapiro(gdp_complete) print(f"W = {test_normalite.statistic:.4f}, p-value = {test_normalite.pvalue:.3g}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` n = 170 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index-en_files/figure-html/shapiro-gdp-output-2.png){#shapiro-gdp width=663 height=375} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` W = 0.8296, p-value = 8.21e-13 ``` ::: ::: ### Example 4: testing the normality of `lex` ::: {#cell-shapiro-lex .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 10 lex_complete = data_2025['lex'].dropna() print("n =", len(lex_complete)) plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4)) plt.hist(lex_complete, bins=30, color="steelblue", edgecolor="white", density=False) plt.title('Distribution of life expectancy across countries') plt.xlabel('Life expectancy (years)') plt.ylabel('Number of countries') plt.tight_layout() plt.show() test_normalite = stats.shapiro(lex_complete) print(f"W = {test_normalite.statistic:.4f}, p-value = {test_normalite.pvalue:.3g}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` n = 170 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index-en_files/figure-html/shapiro-lex-output-2.png){#shapiro-lex width=663 height=374} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` W = 0.9583, p-value = 5.9e-05 ``` ::: ::: ## Parametric or non-parametric? ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} ```{=html}

``` [Open the video](https://mediaserver.unige.ch/play/319458). ::: ::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"} *Normality of the data. This video is available in the HTML version of the course.* ::: **Parametric tests** make assumptions about the distribution of the data or the residuals, often assuming normality. They generally have good power when these assumptions are reasonably satisfied. **Non-parametric tests** make fewer distributional assumptions and are often based on ranks. Their power relative to parametric tests depends on the data distribution and the assumptions of the tests being compared. | Question | Parametric | Non-parametric | |----------|------------|----------------| | Comparing 2 independent groups | Student’s t-test | Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney | | Comparing more than 2 groups | ANOVA | Kruskal–Wallis | | Testing normality | Shapiro–Wilk | - | Do not base the choice solely on a normality test. Also examine the histograms, extreme values, sample sizes and assumptions of the test you are considering. ### Testing the normality of all quantitative variables ::: {#cell-normality-all-numeric .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 11 variables_quantitatives = data_2025.select_dtypes(include="number").columns lignes = [] for variable in variables_quantitatives: x = data_2025.loc[np.isfinite(data_2025[variable]), variable] # Use the same limits as in the R version. if 3 <= len(x) <= 5000 and x.nunique() >= 3: test = stats.shapiro(x) W, p_value = test.statistic, test.pvalue conclusion = ( 'Normality rejected' if p_value < 0.05 else 'Normality not rejected' ) else: W, p_value = np.nan, np.nan conclusion = 'Test not applicable' lignes.append({"variable": variable, "n": len(x), "W": W, "p_value": p_value, "conclusion": conclusion}) resultats_normalite = pd.DataFrame(lignes) display(resultats_normalite) ``` ::: {#normality-all-numeric .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` [Open the video](https://mediaserver.unige.ch/play/319450). ::: ::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"} *Comparing means and understanding ANOVA. This video is available in the HTML version of the course.* ::: Here we compare **Europe** and **Africa**. ### Life expectancy in European and African countries ::: {#hist-lex-europe-africa .cell fig-height='4.5' fig-width='9' execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 13 europe_afrique = data_2025.loc[ data_2025["region"].isin(["europe", "africa"]) ].copy() # The plots and both tests use the same non-missing values. europe_afrique = europe_afrique.dropna(subset=["lex", "region"]) display(europe_afrique.groupby("region")["lex"].agg(["count", "mean", "std"])) bornes = np.histogram_bin_edges(europe_afrique["lex"], bins=20) fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4), sharex=True) for ax, region in zip(axes, ["africa", "europe"]): valeurs = europe_afrique.loc[europe_afrique["region"] == region, "lex"] ax.hist(valeurs, bins=bornes, color="steelblue", edgecolor="white") ax.set_title(region) ax.set_xlabel('Life expectancy (years)') ax.set_ylabel('Number of countries') fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {#hist-lex-europe-africa-1 .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
count mean std
region
africa 52 66.171731 5.181807
europe 43 79.734419 3.208471
``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index-en_files/figure-html/hist-lex-europe-africa-output-2.png){#hist-lex-europe-africa-2 width=854 height=374} ::: ::: ### Student’s t-test We compare the means of the two groups. The hypotheses are: - H0: mean life expectancy is the same in Europe and Africa; - H1: mean life expectancy differs between the two regions. The classical Student’s t-test assumes independent observations, approximate normality within each group and equal variances. Here, `equal_var=True` explicitly requests the classical version of the test. ::: {#student-europe-africa .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 14 # Use the alphabetical group order used by R. lex_afrique = europe_afrique.loc[europe_afrique["region"] == "africa", "lex"] lex_europe = europe_afrique.loc[europe_afrique["region"] == "europe", "lex"] test_student = stats.ttest_ind(lex_afrique, lex_europe, equal_var=True) print(f"t = {test_student.statistic:.3f}, p-value = {test_student.pvalue:.3g}") print("Degrees of freedom:", test_student.df) print('Mean difference Africa − Europe (years):', round(lex_afrique.mean() - lex_europe.mean(), 3)) intervalle = test_student.confidence_interval(confidence_level=0.95) print(f"95% confidence interval: [{intervalle.low:.3f}, {intervalle.high:.3f}]") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` t = -14.949, p-value = 1.82e-26 Degrees of freedom: 93.0 Mean difference Africa − Europe (years): -13.563 95% confidence interval: [-15.364, -11.761] ``` ::: ::: ### The Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney test This non-parametric test compares the ranks of observations in the two groups. It does not require normality. Here, `mannwhitneyu()` compares two independent groups using a normal approximation and continuity correction, as in the R code. Python labels the statistic U and R labels it W, but they represent the same calculation when the groups are in the same order. ::: {#wilcoxon-europe-africa .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 15 test_wilcoxon = stats.mannwhitneyu( lex_afrique, lex_europe, alternative="two-sided", method="asymptotic", use_continuity=True ) print(f"U = {test_wilcoxon.statistic:.1f}, p-value = {test_wilcoxon.pvalue:.3g}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` U = 39.0, p-value = 7.38e-16 ``` ::: ::: > The Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney test is often described as a comparison of distributions. More specifically, it tests for a shift in ranks. Interpreting it as a comparison of medians requires, in particular, distributions with similar shapes. ## Comparing more than 2 means ### Life expectancy in the four regions ::: {#hist-lex-four-regions .cell fig-height='7' fig-width='10' execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 16 ordre_regions = ["africa", "americas", "asia", "europe"] four_regions = data_2025.loc[ data_2025["region"].isin(ordre_regions) ].dropna(subset=["lex", "region"]).copy() display(four_regions.groupby("region")["lex"].agg(["count", "mean", "std"])) # Use equally spaced bins on the log scale, as in the R version. bornes = np.geomspace(four_regions["lex"].min(), four_regions["lex"].max(), 21) couleurs = ["#D98C45", "#4682B4", "#55A868", "#9B6DB0"] fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(9, 6), sharex=True) for ax, region, couleur in zip(axes.flat, ordre_regions, couleurs): valeurs = four_regions.loc[four_regions["region"] == region, "lex"] ax.hist(valeurs, bins=bornes, color=couleur, edgecolor="white") ax.set_xscale("log") ax.set_xticks([50, 60, 70, 80, 90]) ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(ScalarFormatter()) ax.minorticks_off() ax.set_title(region) ax.set_xlabel('Life expectancy (years, log scale)') ax.set_ylabel('Number of countries') fig.tight_layout() plt.show() groupes_lex = [four_regions.loc[four_regions["region"] == r, "lex"] for r in ordre_regions] fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5)) boites = ax.boxplot(groupes_lex, patch_artist=True, showfliers=False) rng = np.random.default_rng(123) for i, (valeurs, couleur, boite) in enumerate( zip(groupes_lex, couleurs, boites["boxes"]), start=1): boite.set_facecolor(couleur) boite.set_alpha(0.7) ax.scatter(i + rng.uniform(-0.15, 0.15, len(valeurs)), valeurs, color=couleur, alpha=0.5, s=16) ax.set_xticks(range(1, 5), ordre_regions) ax.set_title('Life expectancy by region') ax.set_ylabel('Life expectancy (years)') fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {#hist-lex-four-regions-1 .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index-en_files/figure-html/hist-lex-four-regions-output-2.png){#hist-lex-four-regions-2 width=855 height=566} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index-en_files/figure-html/hist-lex-four-regions-output-3.png){#hist-lex-four-regions-3 width=759 height=470} ::: ::: ### ANOVA tests whether all the means can be considered equal - H0: the four regions have the same mean life expectancy; - H1: at least one mean differs. ::: {#cell-anova-lex .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 17 modele_anova = ols("lex ~ C(region)", data=four_regions).fit() tableau_anova = anova_lm(modele_anova, typ=1) display(tableau_anova) ``` ::: {#anova-lex .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: A significant ANOVA result tells us that at least one mean differs, but not which one. Tukey’s post-hoc test allows us to explore pairwise differences: ```{=typst} #block(breakable: false)[ ``` ::: {#tukey-posthoc .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 18 test_tukey = pairwise_tukeyhsd( endog=four_regions["lex"], groups=four_regions["region"], alpha=0.05 ) print(test_tukey.summary()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Multiple Comparison of Means - H0: the groups have comparable rank distributions; - H1: at least one group differs. ::: {#kruskal-wallis-density .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 20 test_kruskal = stats.kruskal(*groupes_lex) print(f"H = {test_kruskal.statistic:.3f}, p-value = {test_kruskal.pvalue:.3g}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` H = 93.585, p-value = 3.72e-20 ``` ::: ::: ## Independence between two categorical variables: the χ² test The previous tests compared a quantitative variable across groups. The **chi-square test of independence** looks for an association between **two categorical variables**, using a table of counts. ### The question and the variables Is the proportion of countries with a life expectancy of at least 75 years the same in all four regions? We use the same dataset: - `region`: the region of the world; - `classe_lex`: life expectancy below 75 years, or at least 75 years. The threshold of 75 years is chosen for this exercise before looking at the result. Turning a quantitative variable into categories loses information. Here, we do so to illustrate the chi-square test. ### Preparing the data Each country must appear only once and belong to a single category for each variable. Missing values are excluded. ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} ```{=html}

This video is available in the HTML version of the course.* ::: ::: {#cell-chi2-prepare .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 21 donnees_chi2 = four_regions.loc[np.isfinite(four_regions["lex"])].copy() donnees_chi2["region"] = pd.Categorical( donnees_chi2["region"], categories=ordre_regions ) classes_lex = ['Under 75 years', '75 years or older'] donnees_chi2["classe_lex"] = pd.Categorical( np.where(donnees_chi2["lex"] < 75, classes_lex[0], classes_lex[1]), categories=classes_lex, ordered=True ) display(donnees_chi2[["name", "region", "lex", "classe_lex"]].head(10)) ``` ::: {#chi2-prepare .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Each cell contains a count of countries, not a percentage. ::: {#chi2-contingency .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 22 tableau_chi2 = pd.crosstab(donnees_chi2["region"], donnees_chi2["classe_lex"]) # Display counts and totals. totaux = tableau_chi2.copy() totaux["Total"] = totaux.sum(axis=1) totaux.loc["Total"] = totaux.sum(axis=0) display(totaux) # Calculate proportions within each region. proportions = tableau_chi2.div(tableau_chi2.sum(axis=1), axis=0) display((100 * proportions).round(1)) ``` ::: {#chi2-contingency-1 .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

The proportions in the two categories are the same across regions in the reference population. - **H1:** the two variables are associated. At least one region has a different distribution across the categories. Under H0, the expected count in each cell is: $$ E_{ij} = \frac{\text{total for row } i \times \text{total for column } j} {\text{overall count}} $$ The test statistic measures the discrepancy between the observed and expected counts: $$ \chi^2 = \sum_{i,j} \frac{(O_{ij} - E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}} $$ Larger discrepancies produce a larger statistic. For a table with four regions and two categories, the degrees of freedom are $(4-1)(2-1)=3$. ### Checking the expected counts The chi-square approximation requires sufficiently large expected counts. A common rule of thumb is: - no expected count below 1; - at least 80% of the expected counts equal to or greater than 5. These conditions concern the **expected counts**, not the observed counts. ::: {#cell-chi2-expected .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 24 effectifs_attendus = pd.DataFrame( stats.contingency.expected_freq(tableau_chi2), index=tableau_chi2.index, columns=tableau_chi2.columns ) display(effectifs_attendus.round(2)) conditions_chi2 = ( (effectifs_attendus.to_numpy() >= 1).all() and (effectifs_attendus.to_numpy() >= 5).mean() >= 0.80 ) print(conditions_chi2) ``` ::: {#chi2-expected .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` True ``` ::: ::: ### Running the test If the expected counts are large enough, we use the usual approximation. Otherwise, we calculate a p-value using Monte Carlo simulation. ::: {#chi2-test .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 25 if conditions_chi2: test_chi2 = stats.chi2_contingency(tableau_chi2, correction=False) methode_chi2 = 'Pearson chi-square, asymptotic approximation' else: # Simulate tables with fixed margins, as in R’s chisq.test(). simulation = stats.MonteCarloMethod( n_resamples=99999, rng=np.random.default_rng(123) ) test_chi2 = stats.chi2_contingency( tableau_chi2, correction=False, method=simulation ) methode_chi2 = 'Pearson chi-square, simulated p-value' print(f"χ² = {test_chi2.statistic:.3f}, p-value = {test_chi2.pvalue:.3g}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` χ² = 67.067, p-value = 1.81e-14 ``` ::: ::: For a 2 × 2 table with small expected counts, Fisher’s exact test is another common option: `stats.fisher_exact(tableau)`. ### Interpreting the result ::: {#chi2-interpretation .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 26 print('Method:', methode_chi2) print('Chi-square statistic:', round(test_chi2.statistic, 2)) print(f"p-value : {test_chi2.pvalue:.3g}") if test_chi2.pvalue < 0.05: print('At the 5% significance level, we reject H0:', 'the data indicate an association between region', 'and life expectancy category.') else: print('At the 5% significance level, we do not reject H0:', 'the data do not provide sufficient evidence of an association.', 'This does not establish independence.') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Method: Pearson chi-square, asymptotic approximation Chi-square statistic: 67.07 p-value : 1.81e-14 At the 5% significance level, we reject H0: the data indicate an association between region and life expectancy category. ``` ::: ::: A significant result indicates an **association**. It does not establish that region causes the differences in life expectancy. ### Measuring the strength of association: Cramér’s V The p-value does not measure the strength of the association. **Cramér’s V** complements the test and ranges from 0 to 1. A value close to 0 indicates a weak association. Its importance should be interpreted in the context of the study. ::: {#cell-chi2-cramer .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Block 27 n_chi2 = tableau_chi2.to_numpy().sum() v_cramer = np.sqrt( test_chi2.statistic / (n_chi2 * min(np.array(tableau_chi2.shape) - 1)) ) display(pd.DataFrame([{'number_of_countries': n_chi2, "V_Cramer": v_cramer}])) ``` ::: {#chi2-cramer .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Moreover, these data are a collection of countries with available information, rather than a random sample. Statistical inference therefore remains conditional on these assumptions. The conclusions apply only to the countries retained after filtering and to the categories defined by the 75-year threshold. # Interpreting tests We can follow four steps when interpreting a statistical test: 1. **State H0 and H1** before looking at the result. 2. **Check the test assumptions** and examine the data graphically. 3. **Read the p-value** and compare it with the significance level $\alpha$, often set to 0.05. 4. **Interpret the effect in context**, going beyond “significant” or “not significant”. Statistical significance alone does not tell us how important a difference is in practice. It is also useful to examine means or medians, variability, effect sizes and confidence intervals. # Summary: which test should we choose? The choice depends first on the types of variables, the question being asked and whether the observations are independent or paired. The table below concerns comparisons of independent groups. | Aim | Variables | Groups | Main assumptions and considerations | Test | |--------------------|--------------------|---------------|-------------------------|--------------------| | Test normality | One quantitative variable or a set of residuals | - | 3 to 5,000 values; supplement with a histogram and a Q–Q plot | Shapiro–Wilk | | Compare two means | One quantitative and one categorical variable | 2 | Independent observations; approximate normality within groups or sufficiently large samples; sensitivity to extreme values | Welch’s t-test; Student’s t-test if equal variances are justified | | Compare two distributions using ranks | One quantitative or ordinal variable and one categorical variable | 2 | Independent observations; similar distribution shapes to interpret a difference in location | Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney | | Compare several means | One quantitative and one categorical variable | More than 2 | Independent observations; approximately normal residuals; comparable variances | Classical ANOVA; Welch’s ANOVA if variances differ | | Compare several distributions using ranks | One quantitative or ordinal variable and one categorical variable | More than 2 | Independent observations; similar distribution shapes to interpret a difference in location | Kruskal–Wallis | | Test an association between categories | Two categorical variables | At least 2 categories per variable | Independent country observations; sufficiently large expected counts | Chi-square test of independence | | Test an association with small counts | Two categorical variables | At least 2 categories per variable | Examine the expected counts and the dimensions of the table | Fisher’s exact test, particularly for 2 × 2 tables, or a chi-square test with a simulated p-value | ```{=typst} #block(breakable: false)[ ``` **Key points:** - Do not choose a test solely on the basis of Shapiro–Wilk. - When comparing means, examine distributions within groups and model residuals, rather than just the overall distribution. - The chi-square test uses counts, not percentages directly. - A significant association does not demonstrate causality. - Always complement the p-value with graphs and a measure of the size of the effect. ```{=typst} ] ``` # Questions about this session {#questions-session-04} If a concept is still unclear, you would like to explore an example further, or you have any other question, feel free to ask it in the SpeakUp space below (anonymously or not).
